bottleneck: Experiments show brain activity predicting decisions seconds before conscious awareness, challenging the notion of free will — yet what these readiness signals actually encode is debated. They may reflect pre-decision bias or attention rather than the decision itself, and the laboratory choices studied (when to move a finger) bear little resemblance to deliberated moral choices. Whether decisions are determined, stochastic, or genuinely chosen matters for moral responsibility, law, and psychiatry, but neuroscience can describe the neural precursors without settling the metaphysics. The data consistently outrun the interpretation, and each side reads its philosophy into the same traces.
current_state: Libet-style findings replicate with nuances — predictive signals exist but are weaker and more ambiguous than early claims. Philosophers and neuroscientists still disagree on what they mean for agency.

sources.title: Why Neuroscience Cannot Dissolve the Hard Problem of Consciousness

title: Decision neuroscience cannot settle free will
why_it_blocks: Law, ethics, and psychiatry all assume agency, and courts increasingly hear neuroscientific evidence about responsibility. If neuroscience undermines free will without replacing it, the foundations of blame, punishment, and treatment need rebuilding on uncertain ground.
